card.name: Saya
card.tagline: Bolivia's Afro-Andean dance — the Yungas mountain communities' polyrhythmic tradition, hidden for 400 years, now reclaiming national stages.
card.profile: Saya is the foundational music and dance of the Afro-Bolivian community of the Yungas — the descendants of enslaved Africans brought to Bolivia's silver mines starting in the 16th century, who eventually settled in the cloud-forest valleys north of La Paz. The dance is polyrhythmic and call-and-response, performed by men and women in distinct rows to the deep beat of the caja (drum), guancha (scraper), and accompanying call-singer. Long marginalized within Bolivian national folklore, saya has gained increasing visibility since the 1980s as the Afro-Bolivian community has organized around cultural recognition.
card.insight: Bolivia's 2009 constitution — the first Andean constitution to formally recognize Afro-Bolivian identity as one of the country's founding peoples — was signed alongside national tributes to saya as a cultural heritage of the Bolivian state. Today the Yungas town of Tocaña hosts an annual Festival of Saya, and the dance is performed at every major Bolivian national celebration alongside the formerly more dominant Andean folkloric forms.
